---

I added a `--dry-run` flag to my reporting app a few months ago. Not because I had a grand plan. Just remembered how Subversion had one, thought "that was useful."

Ended up using it literally every day since.

If you've worked with command-line tools, you know that moment - cursor hovering over Enter, running through a mental checklist. "Did I check the config? Is the database connection right? Am I about to accidentally email 10,000 customers?"

`--dry-run` removes that pause entirely.

It shows you exactly what WOULD happen without actually doing anything. No changes. No side effects. Safe to run whenever, however many times you want.

Here's what surprised me: I thought I'd use it for debugging. Instead, I use it for confidence.

Before starting work each morning, I run it. Not to test anything specific - just to confirm the world is as I expect. Config's correct. Files are where they should be. Database is accessible. Takes 2 seconds. Removes the mental overhead of "is everything okay?"

When I'm making changes, I use it for instant feedback. I can modify a date in a config file and immediately see what reports would generate - without waiting for actual report generation (which takes minutes).

The cost is minimal. A few `if (dryRun)` checks scattered through the code. The benefits keep accumulating.

Not every application needs this. If you're building reactive systems that wait for events, `--dry-run` doesn't make much sense. But for command-line tools that create, modify, or move things? It's a small feature that removes a surprising amount of cognitive load.

We talk a lot about sophisticated architecture and clever algorithms. Sometimes the most valuable features are the simple ones that let you move faster because you're less afraid of breaking things.

What small feature in your codebase has had an outsized impact on your daily workflow?
